metadata.title: Agent Swarms.
metadata.note: Concept explainer (framework-first, built to pass PROOF). Narrator Muskan, @HumanitariansAI, banner 'AI, Explained'. ONE reusable idea: an agent swarm is many agents that divide a task, work in parallel with separate contexts, and converge on one answer — it wins only when the work actually DECOMPOSES (parallel subtasks, specialized roles, diverse attempts), and loses when it doesn't, because coordination costs more than it buys. The reusable test the viewer leaves with: can you name the split and the merge? If not, use one good agent. Non-dating: no product or framework names, no versions; cost scales ×N, coordination/convergence is the trade, decomposition is the test. Bookends render via remotion (ClaudeComposerAsk, ClaudeVerdictArtifact, ClaudeTitleOutro) at --scale=2 (4K); body B01-B04 are house-style 4K PIL cards (make_cards.py) — kinds versus, grid, example, grid. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW: multi-agent/swarm claims are standard and accurate (orchestrator-worker, parallelism, specialization, ensembling/diversity, coordination overhead, ×N cost, convergence/merging difficulty).

beats.narration_text: Hey, I'm Muskan. One AI agent can only do so much: one context window, one task at a time, one point of view. So people are wiring many agents together to work as a group. That's an agent swarm. But the real question isn't how to build one. It's when more agents actually help, and when they just get in each other's way.

props.command: When do many AI agents actually beat one good agent — and when are they just overhead?
output: one agent: serial, one context, one view
the test: does the task actually split?

beats.narration_text: Here's the shift. A single agent works serially, in one context, with one perspective. A swarm is many agents coordinating toward one goal, so they can work in parallel, hold separate contexts, and take on different roles. But that word, coordinating, is doing a lot of work. A swarm isn't just more agents. It's agents that can divide the task, share what they find, and converge on an answer.

card.title: One Agent, or a Swarm?
card.subtitle: the reframe
card.caption: a swarm isn't just more agents — it's agents that divide, share, and converge
card.footer: MANY AGENTS · ONE GOAL · IF THEY COORDINATE

beats.narration_text: Done right, three things get better. Parallelism: split a job into pieces and run them at once. Specialization: a researcher, a coder, a critic, each good at its own part. And diversity: several agents attempt it independently, and you combine or vote, which beats any single try. More hands, more angles, more speed.

card.title: Why a Swarm Wins.
card.subtitle: when the work splits
card.caption: split the job, give each piece to the agent best at it

beats.narration_text: Watch it on a report. One agent, the orchestrator, breaks the goal into sections and hands them out. A research agent gathers sources, a writer drafts, a fact-checker verifies each claim, all at the same time. The orchestrator merges their work, and a critic agent reads the whole thing and sends back fixes. Five agents, one brief, each doing the part it's best at.

show.at: each doing the part it's best at

card.title: One Brief, Five Agents.
card.subtitle: orchestrator → workers → critic
card.answer: research + write + fact-check (in parallel) → merge → a critic reviews → done
card.caption: the orchestrator divides and merges; each agent does the part it's best at
card.footer: DIVIDE · WORK IN PARALLEL · MERGE · REVIEW

beats.narration_text: But a swarm is not free, and it's often the wrong tool. Every agent costs tokens, so five agents can mean five times the bill. They can duplicate work, or contradict each other, and converging them is its own hard problem. And if the task doesn't actually split, a swarm is just a slow, expensive way to do what one good agent could have done alone. So the test, before you reach for a swarm: does this genuinely decompose?

card.title: Not a Free Lunch.
card.subtitle: when a swarm is the wrong tool

items.quote: merging them is its own problem
only if the task actually splits

card.caption: if the work doesn't decompose, a swarm is a slow, costly way to do one agent's job
card.footer: NO CLEAN SPLIT → ONE GOOD AGENT WINS

beats.narration_text: So, an agent swarm: many agents that divide a task, work in parallel, and converge on one answer. It wins on jobs that truly split into parallel or specialized parts, and loses on jobs that don't, where the coordination costs more than it buys. Reach for it when the work comes apart cleanly. Not before.

artifactLines: A swarm is many agents that divide a task, work in parallel with separate contexts, and converge on one answer.
It wins when the work decomposes: parallel subtasks, specialized roles, or diverse attempts you combine.
Coordination is the cost: ×N tokens, duplicate or conflicting work, and merging is its own hard problem.
The test before reaching for a swarm: can you name the split and the merge? If not, use one good agent.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take a task you'd give an AI. Ask: can I split this into pieces that run independently, and then combine them? If yes, who coordinates, and how do they agree at the end? And if you can't name the split and the merge, you don't need a swarm. You need one good agent.
